key: Match each finding to its drug by mechanism: ACE inhibitors fail the fetal kidney, warfarin blocks bone proteins, phenytoin stunts fingertips, alcohol flattens the midface, lithium displaces the tricuspid valve, thalidomide halts limb buds, tetracycline binds calcium in teeth and isotretinoin disrupts neural crest.
items: Without angiotensin II the fetal efferent arteriole cannot hold filtration pressure, so the kidneys stop producing urine.
Fetal urine makes most of the amniotic fluid after the first trimester, so renal failure leaves very little fluid.
Too little amniotic fluid compresses the fetal chest and stops lung growth, which causes respiratory failure at birth.
Warfarin blocks vitamin K carboxylation of bone and cartilage proteins, so the nasal bridge fails to form in weeks 6 to 12.
Abnormal cartilage calcification gives punctate dots at the ends of long bones on radiographs, called chondrodysplasia punctata.
Later exposure lowers the vitamin K-dependent clotting factors in the fetus, so the fragile brain can bleed.
Underdeveloped fingertips and nails are the hallmark of the fetal hydantoin syndrome.
This is the named pattern of phenytoin embryopathy, with growth restriction, coarse facies and underdeveloped distal digits.
Alcohol disrupts midface growth, so the groove between the nose and upper lip is flat.
The same midface hypoplasia flattens the vermilion border of the upper lip.
Leading preventable cause of intellectual disability
Ethanol kills neurons and disrupts their migration at every stage, so brain injury occurs even when the face looks near normal.
First-trimester lithium is linked to this tricuspid valve malformation, though the absolute risk is small.
The tricuspid valve is displaced downward, so part of the right ventricle functions as an enlarged right atrium.
Thalidomide blocks limb bud outgrowth in weeks 4 to 8, leaving flipper-like limbs.
Absent or shortened long bones put the hands and feet close to the body wall.
The drug binds calcium and deposits in developing teeth, staining them permanently.
Drug laid down with calcium in forming teeth
Tetracyclines chelate calcium, so they are laid down in teeth that mineralize after the first trimester and stain them permanently.
Retinoic acid disrupts the neural crest cells that form the ear and palate.
Neural crest cells also septate the outflow tract, so truncus and tetralogy-type defects arise.
